analysis.summary_en: This review explores the development and clinical application of mRNA-based therapies, particularly in the context of rabies virus and rabies disease. It highlights the historical breakthroughs in mRNA stability and delivery, such as the use of modified nucleosides and lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which have enabled the successful use of mRNA in vaccines and therapeutic applications. The study emphasizes the potential of mRNA to treat genetic disorders and infectious diseases, with specific examples including the approval of an mRNA-based therapy for polyneuropathy associated with hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis. Despite these advancements, the high costs of mRNA-based therapies have limited their widespread use. The findings demonstrate the safety and efficacy of mRNA delivery systems, providing a foundation for future research and applications in precision medicine.

title: Dopamine release-associated striatal blood oxygenation and whole-brain dynamics during associative learning

source_records.title: Dopamine release-associated striatal blood oxygenation and whole-brain dynamics during associative learning
Dopamine release-associated striatal blood oxygenation and whole-brain dynamics during associative learning

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: Dopaminergic signaling in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) is central to reward-based learning, but its relationship to brain-wide hemodynamics remains unclear. Using concurrent fMRI and dopamine photometry in awake, behaving mice, we reveal that associative learning induces a gradual temporal shift in NAc blood oxygenation responses that mirrors dopamine release dynamics. This shift emerges with cue-reward learning and extends across a distributed network encompassing the lateral septal complex, as well as prefrontal, insular, and hypothalamic regions. Further, dopamine transients tightly correspond with local blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signals, and variations in reward value modulate delayed BOLD responses in both the NAc and additional subcortical structures. Regressing out the measured dopaminergic signal abolishes this reward-related modulation, suggesting that BOLD signals track dopaminergic reward prediction. These findings reveal a close relationship between dopamine signaling and widespread changes in brain activity during learning. MATERIALS AND METHODSAnimalsAll procedures were conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the National Institutes of Health and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at Columbia University (AC-AABT2650). Eighteen male C57/BL6 mice (2–3 months old) were used in this study. Male mice were used exclusively in this study. Although sex differences in associative learning and dopaminergic signaling have been reported in rats (69) and thus could potentially extend to mice, this study was restricted to a single sex in order to reduce inter-subject variability while establishing and validating this technically demanding experimental paradigm. Awake fMRI combined with longitudinal behavioral training and stereotactic viral targeting is highly sensitive to variability in body size, movement, behavioral vigor, and surgical reproducibility. Given the lack of methodological precedent for this approach, experimental consistency was prioritized by maintaining uniform age, training procedures, hardware, and sex. Future studies in female mice are required to determine whether sex differences shape dopaminergic dynamics, fMRI responses, and learning-related shifts in neural responses.Mice were implanted with MRI-compatible head posts and housed in a reversed 12-hour light/dark cycle. After a recovery period of 7–10 days, during which the mice returned to their preoperative weight, a 7–10 day water restriction regime began. The mice were initially given water access for 120 s per day, gradually decreasing to 90 s until they stabilized at approximately 85% of their initial weight. Additional water access time was provided if the mice did not meet the 85% weight criteria, all 18 mice dedicated for learning task reached weight criteria within 10 days. Once weight stabilization was achieved, the scanning sessions commenced.Head-post surgeryFor head fixation, mice were implanted with custom-made MRI-compatible head posts. Pre-operatively, the mice received extended-release Buprenorphine (Buprenorphine XR) for analgesia. They were then anesthetized with isoflurane (1.5–2.5%) and given additional local analgesia (Marcaine) before making any incisions. The scalp and periosteum layer were removed to expose the skull, and the head post was secured using dental cement (Metabond, Parkell). In some cases, an additional layer of dental cement (Paladur, Heraeus Kulzer) was applied to enhance homogeneity and reduce susceptibility artifacts.Head fixation and scanner habituationAfter recovery, mice were handled daily for progressively longer periods. Initially, the mice were allowed to sniff the experimenter’s hand, followed by gradually lifting them and letting them explore the experimenter. Subsequently, the mice were introduced to the cradle used for head fixation. After two days of handling, the mice were allowed to enter the head-fixation cylinder. Once inside, the experimenter captured and fixed the head post with fixation forks. The mice were head-fixed for progressively longer durations—1, 2, 5, 8, 15, and finally 25 minutes on consecutive days. During the last two days of habituation, the mice were placed inside the magnet bore, where scanner noises were introduced.Water deliveryWater was delivered using a normally closed Parker Series 3 Miniature Inert Liquid Valve, which was triggered for a preset and calibrated amount of time to deliver 1, 3, or 6 μl of water per trial. Since the valve is not MRI-safe, it was placed outside the MRI room and connected to the experimental setup in the scanner via a 7-meter-long tube. At the start of each scanning day, water was flushed through the tube for 4 minutes to ensure the dissipation of air bubbles. Water was then calibrated by administering 100 drops into a small container, which was weighed to calculate the average water drop volume. Calibration was iteratively adjusted until accurate volumes were achieved.Behavioral pretrainingAlthough the mice were entirely naive to the structure of the experiment and were introduced to the unconditioned stimulus only on the first day of recording, it was crucial to familiarize them with the setup, particularly the water delivery system. On the last day of habituation, at random time points, the mice were given 3 μl water drops from the water spout positioned near their mouths. We ensured that they licked the water drops. If a mouse did not lick, the experimenter gently moved the water spout to touch the mouse’s mouth, prompting the water-deprived mouse to initiate licking. By the end of the last day of habituation, each mouse voluntarily acquired 10 drops of water.Behavioral monitoringTo monitor mice and extract behavioral features, the setup included an MRI-compatible 12 M-i camera (MRC Systems GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany) with an acquisition rate of 29.97 frames per second and a built-in tunable infrared LED to optimize brightness and contrast. The scanner bore is small, preventing the camera from capturing a side view of the mouse. Importantly, tracking tongue protrusion is challenging from a front view since the tongue lacks proper contrast in a grayscale image from that perspective. Therefore, we incorporated a mirror positioned by the mouse’s side and tilted at 45°, allowing the front-view camera to also capture a side view (70).To detect licks, we used an in-house algorithm. Briefly, we performed region of interest (ROI) analysis on the tip of the spout. With the grayscale camera, infrared LED, and black resin setup, the tongue appears bright white on a dark background once protruded. Therefore, when the tongue approaches the designated ROI, the overall brightness of the ROI increases reliably. After estimating the brightness of the ROI across a run, a simple spike-detection approach is employed.Task detailsAfter reaching the weight criterion, all mice participated in the learning task and were scanned using MRI while their behavior was concurrently monitored (n = 18). The learning task consisted of 10 consecutive days of scanning, during which each mouse underwent 100 trials per day (1000 trials per mouse in total). All mice exhibited robust anticipatory licking behavior within 7 days (Fig. 1F; range: 3–7 days; mean = 5.75 days).Learning was assessed at the individual-animal level rather than solely at the group level. A mouse was considered to have learned the cue–reward association if, on days 9 and 10, it exhibited a statistically significant increase in lick rate during cue presentation relative to early training (days 1 and 2). This criterion was evaluated using an unpaired t test comparing lick rate during the cued period in late training (days 9–10; 200 trials) versus early training (days 1–2; 200 trials) for each individual mouse.In the second stage of the experiment, water volume (reward magnitude) was varied. Mice were scanned for at least 5 consecutive days, completing 14–21 runs (mean = 16, SD = 2.04). In each run, mice received 51 trials: 17 trials with a 1 μl water reward, 17 trials with a 3 μl reward, and 17 trials with a 6 μl reward. Five mice did not undergo the learning paradigm and were scanned only during the variable-reward stage, while one mouse was scanned only during the learning paradigm, resulting in a total of 22 mice included in the variable-reward stage.Image acquisitionMRI scans were performed at 9.4 Tesla MRI (Bruker BioSpin, Ettlingen, Germany) using a quadrature 86 mm transmit-only coil (Bruker BioSpin) and a 20 mm loop receive-only coil (Bruker BioSpin). Mice were briefly anesthetized (5% isoflurane) and mounted on the cradle. Water port was adjusted until proper access to water reward was achieved. Each daily session included acquisition of one low-resolution rapid acquisition process with a relaxation enhancement (RARE) T2-weighted structural volume (50 coronal slices, TR/TE 2300/8.5 ms, RARE factor = 4, flip angle = 180°, 200 by 200 by 300 μm3, field of view of 19.2 by 19.2 mm2, matrix size of 96 by 96) and multiple spin-echo echo-planar imaging runs measuring BOLD (TR/TE 2500/13.022 ms, flip angle = 90°, 50 coronal slices, 200 by 200 by 300 μm3, field of view of 14.4 by 9.6 mm2, matrix size of 72 by 48; the imaged volume was framed with four saturation slices to avoid wraparound artifacts). During scanner calibrations and acquisition of anatomical images, mice received random drops of water to keep them calm.Data pre-processing and confound correctionScans were organized according to BIDS format (71). First, raw data underwent noise reduction using Noise reduction with Distribution corrected (NORDIC) PCA (72). Pre-processing was performed on separate runs using Rodent Automated Bold Improvement of EPI Sequences (RABIES) (73). Pre-processing included inhomogeneity correction, motion correction, a rigid registration between functional and anatomical scan per session, non-linear registration between a mouse scanning session anatomical scan and provided RABIES template, a common-space re-sampling to 0.2 by 0.2 by 0.45 mm3. After pre-processing, a visual inspection was performed on all data for quality control, all scans were included in the analyses. Later, pre-processed data was confound-corrected using ICA-AROMA (74), white matter; ventricle; and global signal regression, motion regression, spatial smoothing to 0.5 mm3. Whole-brain temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR), computed following the RABIES pipeline and averaged across animals, demonstrated robust signal quality across cortical and subcortical regions, with expected reductions primarily confined to inferior and ventrolateral boundaries (fig. S2).Anatomical definitionsAll functional scans underwent standard preprocessing, including noise reduction, inhomogeneity correction, and motion correction, followed by registration to the RABIES template atlas. As a result, all scans shared a common anatomical space after preprocessing. Subsequently, anatomical annotations from the Allen Mouse Brain Common Coordinate Framework (CCFv3) were registered to the RABIES template, yielding a unified coordinate system. The nucleus accumbens, and other regions were anatomically defined based on its CCFv3 atlas annotations within this common coordinate space.Determining HRF and shift in HRF responseAfter confirming the mice’s ability to associate the light stimulus with the water reward learning in the scanner, we sought to identify brain regions subserving learning by using fMRI blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) contrast. Prior research highlighted differences between the mouse and human hemodynamic response function (HRF), primarily in response duration (45–47). Consequently, using the human canonical HRF would not accurately capture the true responses within the mouse brain. The mouse HRF, characterized by shorter responses, combined with constraints in increasing the sampling rate due to signal-to-noise issues and relaxation times, results in relatively under-sampled data compared to human studies. These constraints magnify the impact of minor deviations on analysis efficiency significantly. Moreover, studies have shown that the HRF is notably influenced by brain states, affecting factors such as time-to-onset, amplitude, and dispersion (44–47, 50). This adds another layer of uncertainty in accurately characterizing the mouse HRF. Given these factors, it was necessary to comprehensively and reliably characterize task-evoked BOLD responses, considering the unique nuances of the mouse HRF. Therefore, average BOLD response from all runs across all animals was calculated. Afterwards, using SPM’s function, spm_hrf, we fit the BOLD response and found the specific parameters to best fit the response. Then, the time-to-peak parameter in spm_hrf function was gradually tuned to find best-fit-hrf parameters per mouse per learning bin. These parameters were later used for further GLM whole-brain response HRF fitting.Fiber photometry surgeryAdult mice (10–12 weeks old) were anesthetized in an induction chamber with 3–5% isoflurane and then placed in a Kopf stereotaxic frame, where anesthesia was maintained at 1.5–2% isoflurane. The skull was exposed, cleaned, and leveled. full_text_sections.abstract: Dopaminergic signaling in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) is central to reward-based learning, but its relationship to brain-wide hemodynamics remains unclear. Using concurrent fMRI and dopamine photometry in awake, behaving mice, we reveal that associative learning induces a gradual temporal shift in NAc blood oxygenation responses that mirrors dopamine release dynamics. This shift emerges with cue-reward learning and extends across a distributed network encompassing the lateral septal complex, as well as prefrontal, insular, and hypothalamic regions. Further, dopamine transients tightly correspond with local blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signals, and variations in reward value modulate delayed BOLD responses in both the NAc and additional subcortical structures. Regressing out the measured dopaminergic signal abolishes this reward-related modulation, suggesting that BOLD signals track dopaminergic reward prediction. These findings reveal a close relationship between dopamine signaling and widespread changes in brain activity during learning.
full_text_sections.methods: MATERIALS AND METHODSAnimalsAll procedures were conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the National Institutes of Health and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at Columbia University (AC-AABT2650). Eighteen male C57/BL6 mice (2–3 months old) were used in this study. Male mice were used exclusively in this study. Although sex differences in associative learning and dopaminergic signaling have been reported in rats (69) and thus could potentially extend to mice, this study was restricted to a single sex in order to reduce inter-subject variability while establishing and validating this technically demanding experimental paradigm. Awake fMRI combined with longitudinal behavioral training and stereotactic viral targeting is highly sensitive to variability in body size, movement, behavioral vigor, and surgical reproducibility. Given the lack of methodological precedent for this approach, experimental consistency was prioritized by maintaining uniform age, training procedures, hardware, and sex. Future studies in female mice are required to determine whether sex differences shape dopaminergic dynamics, fMRI responses, and learning-related shifts in neural responses.Mice were implanted with MRI-compatible head posts and housed in a reversed 12-hour light/dark cycle. After a recovery period of 7–10 days, during which the mice returned to their preoperative weight, a 7–10 day water restriction regime began. The mice were initially given water access for 120 s per day, gradually decreasing to 90 s until they stabilized at approximately 85% of their initial weight. Additional water access time was provided if the mice did not meet the 85% weight criteria, all 18 mice dedicated for learning task reached weight criteria within 10 days. Once weight stabilization was achieved, the scanning sessions commenced.Head-post surgeryFor head fixation, mice were implanted with custom-made MRI-compatible head posts. Pre-operatively, the mice received extended-release Buprenorphine (Buprenorphine XR) for analgesia. They were then anesthetized with isoflurane (1.5–2.5%) and given additional local analgesia (Marcaine) before making any incisions. The scalp and periosteum layer were removed to expose the skull, and the head post was secured using dental cement (Metabond, Parkell). In some cases, an additional layer of dental cement (Paladur, Heraeus Kulzer) was applied to enhance homogeneity and reduce susceptibility artifacts.Head fixation and scanner habituationAfter recovery, mice were handled daily for progressively longer periods. Initially, the mice were allowed to sniff the experimenter’s hand, followed by gradually lifting them and letting them explore the experimenter. Subsequently, the mice were introduced to the cradle used for head fixation. After two days of handling, the mice were allowed to enter the head-fixation cylinder. Once inside, the experimenter captured and fixed the head post with fixation forks. The mice were head-fixed for progressively longer durations—1, 2, 5, 8, 15, and finally 25 minutes on consecutive days. During the last two days of habituation, the mice were placed inside the magnet bore, where scanner noises were introduced.Water deliveryWater was delivered using a normally closed Parker Series 3 Miniature Inert Liquid Valve, which was triggered for a preset and calibrated amount of time to deliver 1, 3, or 6 μl of water per trial. Since the valve is not MRI-safe, it was placed outside the MRI room and connected to the experimental setup in the scanner via a 7-meter-long tube. At the start of each scanning day, water was flushed through the tube for 4 minutes to ensure the dissipation of air bubbles. Water was then calibrated by administering 100 drops into a small container, which was weighed to calculate the average water drop volume. Calibration was iteratively adjusted until accurate volumes were achieved.Behavioral pretrainingAlthough the mice were entirely naive to the structure of the experiment and were introduced to the unconditioned stimulus only on the first day of recording, it was crucial to familiarize them with the setup, particularly the water delivery system. On the last day of habituation, at random time points, the mice were given 3 μl water drops from the water spout positioned near their mouths. We ensured that they licked the water drops. If a mouse did not lick, the experimenter gently moved the water spout to touch the mouse’s mouth, prompting the water-deprived mouse to initiate licking. By the end of the last day of habituation, each mouse voluntarily acquired 10 drops of water.Behavioral monitoringTo monitor mice and extract behavioral features, the setup included an MRI-compatible 12 M-i camera (MRC Systems GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany) with an acquisition rate of 29.97 frames per second and a built-in tunable infrared LED to optimize brightness and contrast. The scanner bore is small, preventing the camera from capturing a side view of the mouse. Importantly, tracking tongue protrusion is challenging from a front view since the tongue lacks proper contrast in a grayscale image from that perspective. Therefore, we incorporated a mirror positioned by the mouse’s side and tilted at 45°, allowing the front-view camera to also capture a side view (70).To detect licks, we used an in-house algorithm. Briefly, we performed region of interest (ROI) analysis on the tip of the spout. With the grayscale camera, infrared LED, and black resin setup, the tongue appears bright white on a dark background once protruded. Therefore, when the tongue approaches the designated ROI, the overall brightness of the ROI increases reliably. After estimating the brightness of the ROI across a run, a simple spike-detection approach is employed.Task detailsAfter reaching the weight criterion, all mice participated in the learning task and were scanned using MRI while their behavior was concurrently monitored (n = 18). The learning task consisted of 10 consecutive days of scanning, during which each mouse underwent 100 trials per day (1000 trials per mouse in total). All mice exhibited robust anticipatory licking behavior within 7 days (Fig. 1F; range: 3–7 days; mean = 5.75 days).Learning was assessed at the individual-animal level rather than solely at the group level. A mouse was considered to have learned the cue–reward association if, on days 9 and 10, it exhibited a statistically significant increase in lick rate during cue presentation relative to early training (days 1 and 2). This criterion was evaluated using an unpaired t test comparing lick rate during the cued period in late training (days 9–10; 200 trials) versus early training (days 1–2; 200 trials) for each individual mouse.In the second stage of the experiment, water volume (reward magnitude) was varied. Mice were scanned for at least 5 consecutive days, completing 14–21 runs (mean = 16, SD = 2.04). In each run, mice received 51 trials: 17 trials with a 1 μl water reward, 17 trials with a 3 μl reward, and 17 trials with a 6 μl reward. Five mice did not undergo the learning paradigm and were scanned only during the variable-reward stage, while one mouse was scanned only during the learning paradigm, resulting in a total of 22 mice included in the variable-reward stage.Image acquisitionMRI scans were performed at 9.4 Tesla MRI (Bruker BioSpin, Ettlingen, Germany) using a quadrature 86 mm transmit-only coil (Bruker BioSpin) and a 20 mm loop receive-only coil (Bruker BioSpin). Mice were briefly anesthetized (5% isoflurane) and mounted on the cradle. Water port was adjusted until proper access to water reward was achieved. At the population level, there was an increase in anticipatory licking over the learning period, significantly different from baseline lick rates (Fig. 1, E and F (9,170) = 22.43, P < 10−24, one-way ANOVA). At the individual level, all mice demonstrated a significant increase in lick rate triggered by the light by the end of the learning phase (Fig. 1F top, t(398) values >5.16, P values <10−5). A sigmoid fit was used to evaluate the time of learning, with the threshold of learning defined as the sigmoid inflection point. Learning occurred on average at 5.75 ± 1.45 days (mean ± std) at the group level (Fig. 1F bottom right).Associative learning mediates dynamic transition in BOLD responsePhasic dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) has been implicated in signaling reward when it is present prior to learning and in anticipation of it when a stimulus-reward association has been formed (20). Thus, we first sought to examine NAc response throughout the learning process (Fig. 2A). We tracked an indirect measure of neural activity using the fMRI blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) contrast which measures the hemodynamic response. To track brain responses throughout the learning process, we anatomically defined the NAc and extracted the fMRI response. To ensure sufficient signal-to-noise (number of trials) for reliable interpretation, we binned the 10 days into 5 non-overlapping bins. We observed that a response during the delay period emerges during learning (Fig. 2B). Due to the relatively long acquisition time for each whole-brain volume with fMRI, a shift in the hemodynamic response function (HRF) can be indirectly inferred by modeling it with a dual gamma function modeling for all data across all days, varying the time-to-peak parameter. We then estimated the change in time-to-peak for each animal across learning bins (Fig. 2C). We observed a shift in the best-fit HRF, which was initially characterized by later-rising HRFs averaging roughly 1 s to peak relative to reward delivery, which then transitioned to earlier-rising HRFs (∼0.2 s to peak, see Methods for details) over the course of learning (Fig. 2D; one-tailed student t test: t (17) = 4.07, P < 0.001). Importantly, this temporal shift did not simply mirror the emergence of anticipatory licking. Anticipatory licking was already significantly elevated during days 3–4 compared to days 1–2 (Fig. 1E; one-tailed student t test: t (17) = 7.68, P < 10−6), whereas the estimated BOLD time-to-peak was not yet significantly different (Fig. 2D; one-tailed student t-test: t (17) = 1.3, P = 0.106), indicating that the behavioral expression of learning preceded the observed shift in BOLD dynamics.Fig. 2.Associative learning mediates dynamic transition in BOLD and dopamine response in the NAc.(A) Outline of nucleus accumbens overlayed on coronal slices. (B) Average normalized BOLD traces extracted from nucleus accumbens across the five bins of learning. (C) Dual-gamma functions used in order to estimate response time, spanning from earlier peak to later peak after cue presentation. (D) Estimated time to peak of best-fit dual-gamma function, showing a gradual decrease in time to peak. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.005, ****P < 0.001. (E) Graphical depiction of dual imaging technique involving fMRI and fiber-photometry, and viral strategy used to label dopaminergic response. (F) Average normalized GRABDA traces (n = 8). (G) Step functions that vary in time-to-onset that were used to estimate response time, spanning from earlier onset to later onset after cue-presentation. (H) Estimated change of response time compared to first learning bin, both in BOLD signal and GRABDA photometry signal. Kruskal-Wallis test, P = 0.9899. (I) Dynamic shift across whole brain. Mouse cartoon graphical elements in (E) were created in BioRender. Kahn, I. Using a similar approach as for the BOLD signal, we first estimated time-locked responses to stimulus-reward trials across learning bins and noted a stimulus-related increase in DA (Fig. 2F). full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONThe ability to associate a cue with an upcoming reward is an adaptive behavior that enables animals to allocate attention and resources more effectively. However, tracking the neural processes that underlie learning over prolonged periods of time remains challenging. To our knowledge, this study is the first to track brain-wide indirect measures of neural responses in parallel with dopamine-specific responses in the ventral striatum during associative learning. We demonstrate that associative learning is correlated with temporal shifts in BOLD responses in the NAc, which reliably correspond with GRABDA photometry signals. These shifts are not limited to the NAc; the LSx, mPFC, insular cortex and hypothalamus also show prominent changes. Although dynamic shifts in dopaminergic release and neural activity during associative learning have been reported in the NAc (21, 32–34), prefrontal cortex (35), and septal complex (36), our findings are the first to offer a whole-brain, region-unconstrained, concurrent, and spatially localized characterization of the broader network correlated with learning. Notably, our data also implicate the insular cortex and hypothalamus—regions not previously established in this context.Our findings provide evidence that BOLD responses track dopaminergic signaling. We observed a correlation between dopamine release and BOLD signals (Figs. 2H and 3C), suggesting that dopamine release may result in vasodilation either directly or indirectly, although this mechanism has not been directly tested. Given that only supraphysiological dopamine release reliably alters NAc spiking activity (37), and that our results are derived from naturalistic conditions, this is consistent with a potential vasoactive role.However, the directionality of the relationship between NAc dopamine dynamics and BOLD responses remains unresolved. The NAc and VTA form a highly interconnected circuit in which mesolimbic dopamine release can influence NAc activity (28–31), while subsets of NAc MSNs can also regulate VTA activity through inhibitory and disinhibitory pathways that subsequently influence dopaminergic signaling (27, 38). For example, some NAc MSN populations project to VTA GABAergic neurons. Through inhibition of these neurons, such projections can disinhibit dopaminergic cells and thereby influence subsequent dopamine release. All in all, the correspondence observed between dopamine release and BOLD responses may arise from feedforward dopaminergic influences, recurrent NAc–VTA interactions, or a combination of both. The correlational nature of the present study does not allow these possibilities to be dissociated.Still, Li and Jasanoff (39) report minimal effects of dopaminergic signaling on neuronal firing despite measurable changes in BOLD amplitude. It is possible that methodological differences contribute to the differing interpretations. Li and Jasanoff’s experiments were performed under anesthesia and employed dopamine-suppressive contrast agents, prolonged trains of VTA stimulation, and substantially longer measurement windows. These factors may alter endogenous mesolimbic circuit dynamics, including recurrent NAc–VTA interactions, compared to the naturalistic behavioral conditions examined here.Thus, we cannot conclusively rule out either mechanism and instead propose a hybrid model. Notably, our finding that the lowest quartile of GRABDA signals does not impact BOLD when regressed out (Fig. 3C) suggests that there are additional contributors to the BOLD response that are not fully captured by the measured dopaminergic signal. Such contributions may reflect other neural processes, potentially including MSN activity and activity associated with cortico-striatal inputs to D1 or D2 MSNs. These inputs have been shown to elicit positive BOLD responses and are essential for driving motivated behavior (40–43). Moreover, regressing out the dopamine signal did not eliminate the BOLD response in the NAc (Fig. 4I), further supporting a role for other contributors to the shaping of this response.Interpreting learning-related changes in hemodynamic responses benefits from prior work showing that the mouse HRF differs systematically from the canonical human HRF, typically exhibiting faster temporal dynamics and substantial variability across acquisition and physiological conditions (44–47). Measurements in awake mice demonstrate markedly faster hemodynamic responses than under anesthesia (48), underscoring that brain state can shift HRF onset, dispersion, and apparent latency—factors that directly impact GLM efficiency and time-to-peak estimation in rodent fMRI (48–51). These considerations are especially relevant here because our central result is a sub-second shift in the best-fit HRF timing across learning (Fig. 2, C and D), observed in awake mice while holding stimulus timing constant. In parallel, optogenetic fMRI studies in mice have used causal control to characterize BOLD temporal linearity and stimulus-to-response transfer properties, providing a mechanistic foundation for treating mouse HRF timing as a parameter that can meaningfully vary with neural drive and state (52–54). Finally, cross-species work comparing BOLD responses under controlled systemic challenges highlights that species differences in oxygenation and vascular physiology can invert or reshape BOLD responses (55), reinforcing the need for species-appropriate HRF modeling when relating mouse hemodynamics to human fMRI inference (45). An important caveat is that our approach may not capture all regions involved in learning. Some regions may exhibit HRFs that were not modeled, may not produce a reliably detectable hemodynamic response, or suffer from low signal-to-noise, especially in midbrain structures, and regions more susceptible to motion artifacts, such as the midbrain, pons or cerebellum, may not be accurately represented.An additional limitation is that our analyses were performed at the level of the nucleus accumbens as a whole. The core and shell subregions differ in connectivity, physiology, and reward-related function (21, 22, 27, 28, 56–59), and future studies with higher spatial resolution will be required to determine whether the learning-related and outcome-related dynamics described here are differentially expressed across these compartments.Another key contribution of our study is further characterizing the relationship between dopamine and brain-wide BOLD signals. To our knowledge, this relationship has not been examined in a minimally invasive manner in awake, behaving animals. Prior work has suggested mixed effects of dopamine on the striatal BOLD response (31, 39, 40). For example, stimulating D1 or D2 medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the striatum produces distinct BOLD profiles, positive or negative, respectively (40), while different input nuclei elicit varied responses (31). Li and Jasanoff (39) showed that inhibition of D1 or D2 receptors did not significantly alter BOLD amplitude, supporting the hypothesis that dopamine may affect BOLD signals via direct vasoactive mechanisms rather than through post-synaptic metabolic demand. Yet, they also observed widespread BOLD changes after receptor inhibition, suggesting dopamine’s role in modulating neural firing. These complexities make interpreting the BOLD signal challenging.The initial BOLD response in the NAc appears to be tightly associated with phasic dopamine release (Fig. 3, A to C). However, dopaminergic reward prediction error signals—and corresponding BOLD responses—include two distinct components following learning (Figs. 3 and 4). As previously noted (60), dopamine signaling evolves from a broad, unselective response to a more refined signal reflecting subjective value and marginal utility (60, 61). We observed this two-phase pattern in BOLD and GRABDA responses during the variable reward stage – an initial response that did not differ between reward magnitudes followed by a graded response…
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONA significant portion of animal behavior can be distilled to the fundamental act of reward-seeking (1). The ability to form associations between cues and outcomes is critical for enhancing predictability and minimizing harm (2, 3). Classical conditioning, in particular, allows animals to consistently enter a motivated state in response to cues that predict potential rewards (4, 5). This learning process engages multiple brain regions, with the nucleus accumbens (NAc) of the ventral striatum acting as a central hub for the acquisition and expression of cue-reward associations (6). Notably, dopamine release in the NAc is thought to mediate reward-related learning and facilitate motivated responses to incentive cues (7–9).While single-cell recordings are essential for identifying regions-specific functions and establishing temporal causality for behavior, they are unable to provide a brain-wide description at the individual level. As brain function depends on activity across multiple brain regions, it is essential to consider whole-brain dynamics to fully understand the neural mechanisms underlying learning (10). Such an approach can provide a more comprehensive view of brain function and the complex interactions among neural circuits.Task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a well-established technique used in human research for identifying brain regions activated by specific task variables or scheduled events (11). In humans, the NAc has been implicated in cue-reward learning, reward processing, and encoding reward prediction errors (12–16). However, little is known about the brain-wide correlates of dopamine release during learning—particularly regarding learning-related shifts in neural responses and their relationship to the blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signal changes measured using fMRI in the NAc (12, 17, 18).To address this gap, we combined fMRI with dopamine (DA) monitoring in awake, behaving mice engaged in a cue–reward associative learning task. Using the GRABDA fluorescent sensor (19), we recorded NAc dopaminergic dynamics concurrently with whole-brain fMRI. We found that NAc BOLD responses progressively shifted from reward- to cue-aligned activity over the course of learning, closely paralleling the temporal evolution of the dopaminergic signal. Similar temporal dynamics emerged across a distributed network including the lateral septal complex (LSx), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), insular cortex, and hypothalamus, highlighting coordinated brain-wide changes associated with cue–reward learning. Furthermore, dopamine release in the NAc closely tracked local NAc BOLD responses and covaried with activity in several of these same regions, including the mPFC, insular cortex, and hypothalamus. Together, these findings provide a framework for interpreting learning-related BOLD signals in the context of distributed neural and dopaminergic dynamics. To ensure sufficient signal-to-noise (number of trials) for reliable interpretation, we binned the 10 days into 5 non-overlapping bins. We observed that a response during the delay period emerges during learning (Fig. 2B). Due to the relatively long acquisition time for each whole-brain volume with fMRI, a shift in the hemodynamic response function (HRF) can be indirectly inferred by modeling it with a dual gamma function modeling for all data across all days, varying the time-to-peak parameter. We then estimated the change in time-to-peak for each animal across learning bins (Fig. 2C). We observed a shift in the best-fit HRF, which was initially characterized by later-rising HRFs averaging roughly 1 s to peak relative to reward delivery, which then transitioned to earlier-rising HRFs (∼0.2 s to peak, see Methods for details) over the course of learning (Fig. 2D; one-tailed student t test: t (17) = 4.07, P < 0.001). Eighteen male C57/BL6 mice (2–3 months old) were used in this study. Male mice were used exclusively in this study. title_original: Dopamine release-associated striatal blood oxygenation and whole-brain dynamics during associative learning

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the relationship between dopaminergic signaling in the nucleus accumbens and brain-wide hemodynamics during associative learning, as dopaminergic signaling is central to reward-based learning but its relationship to hemodynamics remains unclear.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted on mice, with all procedures approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. By the end of the last day of habituation, each mouse voluntarily acquired 10 drops of water, and all 18 mice dedicated for the learning task reached weight criteria within 10 days.
analysis.methods: During the last two days of habituation, mice were placed inside the magnet bore with scanner noises introduced. Water delivery was controlled using a Parker Series 3 Miniature Inert Liquid Valve, and behavioral monitoring was done with an MRI-compatible 12 M-i camera. Pre-processed data was confound-corrected using ICA-AROMA, white matter; ventricle; and global signal regression, motion regression, and spatial smoothing to 0.5 mm3.
analysis.main_results: Whole-brain temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) demonstrated robust signal quality across cortical and subcortical regions, with expected reductions primarily confined to inferior and ventrolateral boundaries. The mouse HRF, characterized by shorter responses, resulted in relatively under-sampled data compared to human studies. Learning was assessed at the individual-animal level rather than solely at the group level.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the robustness of signal quality across brain regions and the under-sampling of data due to the shorter HRF in mice. This study provides novel insights into the dynamics of brain-wide hemodynamics during associative learning.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the understanding of brain-wide hemodynamic responses during learning processes, which may have implications for the development of more accurate models of neural activity in animal studies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was restricted to a single sex to reduce variability, and the data was under-sampled due to technical constraints. The evidence is moderate, as the study provides detailed observations but lacks broader generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the relationship between dopaminergic signaling in the nucleus accumbens and brain-wide hemodynamics during associative learning. Using mice, the research aimed to understand how these processes interact, employing MRI and behavioral monitoring techniques. The results showed robust signal quality across brain regions and highlighted the under-sampled nature of mouse data due to shorter HRF responses. The authors interpreted these findings as novel insights into neural dynamics during learning, which could inform future studies on brain activity. However, the study's focus on a single sex and technical limitations suggest moderate evidence strength, limiting generalizability.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是在小鼠身上进行的,所有程序均得到机构动物护理和使用委员会的批准。在适应的最后一天结束时,每只小鼠自愿获得 10 滴水,所有 18 只致力于学习任务的小鼠在 10 天内达到了体重标准。
elements_zh.methods: 在适应的最后两天,小鼠被放入磁体孔内,并引入扫描仪噪音。使用 Parker 系列 3 微型惰性液体阀控制供水,并使用兼容 MRI 的 12 M-i 相机进行行为监测。使用 ICA-AROMA、白质对预处理数据进行混杂校正;心室;以及全局信号回归、运动回归和空间平滑至 0.5 mm3。
elements_zh.main_results: 全脑时间信噪比(tSNR)显示出皮质和皮质下区域的稳健信号质量,预期的降低主要限于下边界和腹外侧边界。与人类研究相比,小鼠 HRF 的特点是响应较短,导致数据采样相对不足。学习是在个体动物层面而不是仅仅在群体层面进行评估的。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为证明了跨大脑区域信号质量的稳健性以及由于小鼠 HRF 较短而导致的数据采样不足。这项研究为联想学习期间全脑血流动力学的动态提供了新的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以帮助理解学习过程中全脑血流动力学反应,这可能对动物研究中更准确的神经活动模型的开发产生影响。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于单一性别以减少变异性,并且由于技术限制,数据采样不足。证据是中等的,因为该研究提供了详细的观察结果,但缺乏更广泛的普遍性。

full_text: ABSTRACTIntroductionZoonotic diseases pose risks to human, animal, and ecosystem health; effective management relies on coordinated actions across sectors. Although One Health principles promote collaboration across sectors, operational tools for multisectoral risk assessment (RA) are lacking. Therefore, the Tripartite (FAO, WHO, and WOAH) developed the first‐ever One Health operational tool for Joint Risk Assessment (JRA‐OT), with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. This article describes how information from pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia contributed to informing co‐development of the final JRA process and tool.MethodsThree in‐person meetings with international RA and zoonotic disease experts with a One Health background were convened in Rome, Italy, to co‐develop the methodology (November 2017, September 2018) and incorporate pilot feedback (February 2020). Development criteria included a standard, systematic, qualitative, and multisectoral RA process, facilitating incorporation of expert opinion and sector‐specific RA results. The pilot workshops described here were conducted in Indonesia (March 2018), the United Republic of Tanzania (March 2019), and Georgia (July 2019), and feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat.ResultsThese pilot workshops demonstrated JRA's utility and provided critical information for improvements. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) importance of including all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainers.ConclusionsCo‐development of the JRA using country pilots and expert consultations allowed for field‐testing and iterative improvement of the tool, ensuring incorporation of user requirements, robust methodology for the joint, multisectoral assessment of national zoonotic disease risks, and ownership by the different sectors. The process serves as a model for co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools.Keywords: Joint Operational Tools, One Health, risk assessment, zoonoses Piloting of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) process and tool in countries provided feedback for improvement, evidence‐based estimates of national risks from priority zoonotic diseases, and practical training of national facilitators. The JRA offers simple step‐by‐step guidance to countries wishing to undertake joint qualitative risk assessments. 2.Methods2.1.Initial Tool DevelopmentThe JRA‐OT development began in 2014 and was led by a multisectoral international team of epidemiologists, zoonotic disease experts, and RA experts from six countries in three regions, including many from this team of authors, convened through virtual meetings. All pilots were in‐person and had the same direct and indirect objectives (Table 1). A final in‐person expert consultation was held in Rome, Italy (February 2020), and the JRA‐OT was published in December 2020 [8]. The development timeline is depicted in Figure 2.FIGURE 1Joint Risk Assessment pilot countries.TABLE 1Objectives of the Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) pilot workshops.Direct objectivesIndirect objectives Build capacity through training a pool of national facilitators to operationalize the JRA tool at national and subnational levelsProvide likelihood and impact estimates for risk assessment questions on priority hazardsAssess the usefulness of the JRA and consider its sustained useCollect feedback to improve interim versions of the JRA Enhance coordination and trust among relevant stakeholdersFacilitate official and unofficial communication and information sharing among stakeholdersAdvocate for allocation of resources FIGURE 2Development timeline of the Joint Risk Assessment operational tool.2.2.Pilot WorkshopsFor each of the 15 pilot workshops, all relevant ministries, particularly those responsible for animal health and public health, were encouraged to engage through outreach by FAO and WHO country offices. Tripartite central, regional, and country office staff supported the workshops as external facilitators. All pilots, aside from the Indonesian pilot where the risk framing was conducted during the workshop, followed the six steps, below and in Figure 3, adapted from common RA processes used in public health, animal health, and/or environmental RA: Hazard identification: Technical staff and decision‐makers in engaged ministries (hereafter, “ministries”) agreed on national priority endemic, epidemic, or emerging zoonotic hazards, up to 6 months prior to the workshop. Risk framing: Once the hazards were agreed, ministerial decision‐makers characterized the scope, purpose, and objectives of the assessment on the basis of government strategy and policy to ensure the JRA process remained efficient and focused on critical government needs. Selection of participants and national staff: After Steps 1 and 2, ministries identified participants based on the identified hazards and risk framing and selected staff to facilitate the planning and implementation of the pilot and future JRAs (hereafter, “national facilitators”). A JRA lead was agreed among ministries. High‐level ministerial participation was encouraged for workshop Days 0 and 3. Day 0: National facilitators finalized the risk framing and were trained on the JRA process and tool by the external facilitators. Days 1–2: The JRA was introduced and undertaken by participants, led by the national facilitators and supported by external facilitators. Small groups each focused on one identified hazard using information brought to the workshop and presented the outcome of each step in plenary. Substantial time was dedicated to plenary discussion and questions, covering both the technical assessments and the JRA process itself. Day 3: Each group presented final results in plenary. Participants, including decision‐makers, considered existing national zoonotic disease and One Health infrastructure and options for governance of routine JRA leadership and implementation, and identified what criteria would trigger conducting or updating a JRA.FIGURE 3Schematic of the final Joint Risk Assessment process applied during national JRA pilots. Steps are fully described in WHO et al. [8].2.3.Data Capture, Analysis, and IntegrationFrom each pilot's planning period through to the end of each workshop, constraints, challenges, and proposed solutions gleaned from plenary and group workshop discussions, and verbal feedback from participants and national facilitators were captured in written notes taken by the external facilitators. Five hazards (zoonotic influenza viruses in three different contexts, rabies virus, and Leptospira interrogans) were assessed. As such, Indonesian participants and facilitators found they had to identify the assessment's scope and policy objectives as a first step of the group work. This was time‐consuming and only possible because ministerial decision‐makers were present and engaged to advise. Proactively, the Indonesian organizers initiated a full‐day pre‐pilot meeting of the JRA Secretariat and national technical staff to familiarize national facilitators with the JRA steps and to review the workshop objectives. These included staff from the provinces, and hereafter, the term “national facilitators” is inclusive of subnational staff. The entire team agreed that this pre‐pilot meeting was critical to the success of the workshop as it ensured that national facilitators (1) understood the JRA principles, step‐wise process, and tool; (2) practiced facilitation skills with support from the external facilitators prior to the workshop; and (3) could take a leading role in facilitation the next day. The MoH proposed translating and adapting the tool further for the Indonesian context and embedding JRA within the national and provincial frameworks for zoonoses and other emerging infectious diseases based on the existing infrastructure and legal framework. This would be coordinated centrally by Kemenko PMK in collaboration with MoH, MoA, and Ministry of Environment and Forestry. Political will is now highlighted in the final JRA tool as a key element for enhancing the JRA success.3.1.4.Subnational Involvement for Field‐Context and to Ensure Relevance of OutputsThe proactive inclusion of participants from three provinces in the workshop permitted separate assessments of influenza viruses in three different contexts by participants living in those contexts. This allowed nuanced RA and creation of risk management options specific to their epidemiological and cultural context. It emphasized both that not all risks are national, and that local knowledge is critical to assessment of context‐specific risks. Participants were able to then implement subsequent provincial assessments autonomously.3.1.5.Subsequent JRA Implementation in IndonesiaTo further support subnational JRAs, Indonesia initiated national JRA Training of Trainers (ToTs) activities in 2020 followed by ToTs in 10 provinces in 2021, which benefitted from the clear, stepwise guidance provided by the JRA‐OT. Subsequent JRAs applied the revised final tool and operational process and were conducted for SARS‐CoV‐2 virus (2021), Mycobacterium bovis (2022), avian influenza viruses (2022, 2023), rabies virus (2023), and Nipah virus (2026).3.2.United Republic of TanzaniaThe workshop in the United Republic of Tanzania, hereafter referred to as “Tanzania,” took place 1 year later, in Dar es Salaam on March 25–28, 2019. Tanzania was the first African country to conduct a JRA pilot workshop. Twenty‐four representatives of diverse government agencies, including disaster management, at central and subnational levels (e.g., Zanzibar), the One Health Coordination Desk (OHCD), and academic institutions participated during Days 1–3, whereas the JRA Secretariat, national facilitators, the One Health Coordinator, and the Minister of Health also attended Day 0 for the national facilitator training. Zoonotic influenza virus, Bacillus anthracis, and rabies virus were chosen as priority hazards. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTIntroductionZoonotic diseases pose risks to human, animal, and ecosystem health; effective management relies on coordinated actions across sectors. Although One Health principles promote collaboration across sectors, operational tools for multisectoral risk assessment (RA) are lacking. Therefore, the Tripartite (FAO, WHO, and WOAH) developed the first‐ever One Health operational tool for Joint Risk Assessment (JRA‐OT), with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. This article describes how information from pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia contributed to informing co‐development of the final JRA process and tool.MethodsThree in‐person meetings with international RA and zoonotic disease experts with a One Health background were convened in Rome, Italy, to co‐develop the methodology (November 2017, September 2018) and incorporate pilot feedback (February 2020). Development criteria included a standard, systematic, qualitative, and multisectoral RA process, facilitating incorporation of expert opinion and sector‐specific RA results. The pilot workshops described here were conducted in Indonesia (March 2018), the United Republic of Tanzania (March 2019), and Georgia (July 2019), and feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat.ResultsThese pilot workshops demonstrated JRA's utility and provided critical information for improvements. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) importance of including all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainers.ConclusionsCo‐development of the JRA using country pilots and expert consultations allowed for field‐testing and iterative improvement of the tool, ensuring incorporation of user requirements, robust methodology for the joint, multisectoral assessment of national zoonotic disease risks, and ownership by the different sectors. The process serves as a model for co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools.Keywords: Joint Operational Tools, One Health, risk assessment, zoonoses Piloting of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) process and tool in countries provided feedback for improvement, evidence‐based estimates of national risks from priority zoonotic diseases, and practical training of national facilitators. The JRA offers simple step‐by‐step guidance to countries wishing to undertake joint qualitative risk assessments.

full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionTo address the lack of One Health operational tools to guide joint, multisectoral RA for zoonotic disease threats, the Tripartite co‐developed the JRA‐OT with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. Between 2015 and 2020, feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat to generate the final version [8] published in 2020.Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia were the first to be conducted in their respective geographical regions and generated key lessons that were particularly important for informing the final tool and, thus, were selected for detailed description in this manuscript. There was much overlap across the findings from these countries, suggesting that they also represented countries generally. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health culture from the three countries, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) inclusion of all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of providing clear, stepwise operational guidance and ToTs (Table 3).TABLE 3Summary of key lessons learned or confirmed across pilots and integrated into the final Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) tool and process.Summary of key lessons learned or confirmed through JRA pilotsLesson learned inIndonesiaTanzaniaGeorgiaValue of policy‐level risk framing (in person or online)xxxImportance of political will and leveraging existing One Health culturexxxNeed for subnational engagementxxxImportance of including all relevant sectorsxNecessity of providing clear, stepwise operational guidance and training of trainersxx4.1.Value of Policy‐Level Risk FramingOne of the most important findings across pilots was the need for a formal risk‐framing process led by decision‐makers ahead of the workshop. In Indonesia, participants realized that defining the scope, objectives, and policy priorities during the workshop itself was inefficient and only possible because senior officials were present. Tanzania further demonstrated that risk framing could be conducted effectively through virtual consultations and highlighted the importance of framing each hazard separately. In Georgia, better aligning the hazards and framing with national priorities related to tourism and trade on Day 0 reinforced the importance of strong policy input in hazard selection and framing prior to the workshop.4.2.Importance of Political Will and Leveraging Existing One Health CultureAll three pilots showed that high‐level political commitment and existing multisectoral One Health coordination mechanisms were critical for successful implementation, as proposed by Yopa et al. [14]. Indonesia benefited from strong ministerial engagement and an established One Health governance structure, which later supported national and provincial JRA expansion. Tanzania's politically supported OHCD played a central role in organizing and sustaining JRA activities, whereas ministerial participation throughout the workshop reinforced national ownership. Similarly, Georgia's existing One Health Division within the NCDC facilitated planning, coordination, and policy relevance. Across pilots, political support increased participant engagement, improved alignment with national priorities, and facilitated translating JRA findings into action.4.3.Need for Subnational EngagementThe pilots consistently demonstrated that involving subnational participants improved the relevance and practicality of assessments. During pilots, subnational participants were noted to be especially engaged and motivated to act. In Indonesia, representatives from three provinces assessed influenza risks in their own local contexts, enabling development of tailored risk management strategies and demonstrating that zoonotic risks are often context‐specific rather than purely national. Tanzania identified Zanzibar as a priority setting for future subnational JRAs, highlighting the value of localized implementation. In Georgia, regional participants emphasized differences in rabies epidemiology across areas and proposed immediate use of JRA methods at the subnational level. Overall, the pilots showed that subnational participation strengthens contextual understanding, improves local ownership, and supports implementation of locally relevant mitigation measures.4.4.Inclusion of all Relevant SectorsAnother key lesson was the importance of ensuring representation from all relevant sectors in JRA workshops. Georgia particularly illustrated this challenge when the absence of the wildlife sector limited discussions on rabies risks involving wildlife transmission. This experience demonstrated that gaps in sectoral participation can reduce the completeness and quality of assessments. However, it also showed that the JRA process itself can help identify missing stakeholders and strengthen multisectoral collaboration over time. Across pilots, broad participation from human health, animal health, environment, disaster management, and other sectors was recognized as essential for comprehensive RA and effective One Health coordination for zoonotic diseases.4.5.Necessity of Clear, Stepwise Operational Guidance, and ToTsThe pilots highlighted the need for practical, stepwise operational guidance and strong national facilitation capacity. Indonesia pioneered the Day 0 national facilitator training, which became a standard feature of subsequent JRAs. This training helped facilitators understand the methodology, practice facilitation skills, and eventually lead workshops independently, reducing reliance on external experts. Pilots in Tanzania and Georgia validated the value of this approach, with national facilitators increasingly taking ownership of workshop implementation. The Georgia pilot highlighted the need for clearer guidance on hazard selection and joint risk‐framing procedures that were then added into the tool. Key lessons can be grouped into the following categories: The value of policy‐level risk framingThe importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health structuresThe need for subnational engagementThe importance of all relevant sectors being engaged and presentThe need for clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainersThe JRA pilots demonstrated that effective zoonotic disease RA requires strong integration of technical analysis with policy‐level decision‐making, particularly through early and structured risk framing. Sustained political commitment and established One Health coordination mechanisms were critical enablers of successful JRA implementation and long‐term national ownership. Inclusion of subnational actors and all relevant sectors significantly improved the contextual relevance, completeness, and operational value of RAs.The pilots showed that JRAs can serve not only as technical tools for RA, but also as mechanisms for strengthening multisectoral collaboration, information sharing, and One Health governance. Standardized operational guidance, facilitator training, and nationally led ToTs were essential for building sustainable country capacity and reducing reliance on external support.The JRA was co‐developed iteratively and inclusively across countries, sectors, and scales to meet objectives laid down by national governments and experts in RA and zoonotic diseases to assess risks, and thus models One Health best practice in both content and process and ensures ownership by the different sectors. full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionActions and policies to identify, assess, manage, and reduce risks from zoonotic diseases benefit from functional collaboration and engagement across stakeholders and sectors, including academia, the private sector, local communities, and government ministries responsible for human health, animal health, food safety, wildlife, environment, trade, education, security and disasters, and the economy [1]. Under the International Health Regulations (2005) monitoring and evaluation framework—Joint External Evaluation guidance [2], countries should have the capacity to conduct joint assessments of risk for zoonotic diseases using a One Health approach.In 2014, countries concerned about the potential spread of a zoonotic avian influenza A(H7N9) virus strain in Asia wished to align the results of sectoral risk assessments (RAs) and risk‐related communication messages but encountered challenges in sharing information and conducting RA jointly across sectors. Due to its sensitive nature, information related to zoonotic diseases can potentially influence consumer behavior and/or compromise a country's economy or tourism if made public. Sharing such information between sectors often must be authorized and may be restricted or delayed, especially in the absence of clear sharing mechanisms or policies. Further, although countries could access sector‐specific RA methodologies and processes, they encountered challenges in assessing risks jointly when encountering differing steps and terminology across RA methods and the reluctance of sectors to agree on an approach unfamiliar to them in the absence of expert guidance. These countries requested assistance from the Tripartite [3] to identify and propose a technically sound approach to conducting joint, multisectoral zoonotic disease RA.Technical aspects of estimating risks are, in principle, similar across RA methods, and it is normally possible to incorporate information from other sectors during sector‐specific zoonotic disease RAs. However, each sector‐specific method evolved to achieve different objectives. Consequently, RA methods are operationally different, do not easily align, and do not lend themselves to joint use. Although many institutions and agencies publish RA reports for zoonotic diseases, an extensive search of published guidance for conducting zoonotic disease RA across health‐related disciplines identified only sector‐specific tools available at that time. Further, the guidance from WHO [4], WOAH [5](updated in 2024) and FAO [6](available internally but unpublished at the time) referred to assessment for zoonotic diseases but had been developed exclusively by and for the human health and animal health sectors, respectively. The RA procedures of the Codex Alimentarius Commission [7] were also available but primarily focused on quantitative assessment of contaminants in food and were not practical for use by countries. To fill this gap, the Tripartite convened international RA experts and pilot countries to iteratively co‐develop the first‐ever One Health operational tool for conducting zoonotic disease RA jointly across sectors.The Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) was published as the Joint Risk Assessment Operational Tool (JRA‐OT) in 2020 [8], as one of the operational tools supporting the Tripartite Zoonoses Guide [1]. The JRA‐OT provides a systematic and iterative step‐by‐step process to bring together stakeholders from different sectors. Together, they share expertise, discuss available information, and jointly identify and qualitatively assess risks associated with zoonotic hazards nationally and subnationally, based on strategic policy concerns. and communication messages.Facilitates agreement and ownership of results across sectors, allowing development of nuanced and acceptable management interventions with fewer negative externalities.Prospectively considers strategic policy needs across sectors at national and subnational levels, expediting aligned and contextualized implementation done jointly or separately by each sector.Fosters mutual understanding of perceptions, mandates, constraints, and daily work across sectors, improving communication for future collaborative activities, including emergency title_original: Iterative Co‐Development of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment Operational Process and Tool Through Incorporating Information From Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop an operational tool for Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) to manage zoonotic diseases, as effective multisectoral risk assessment is critical for addressing health risks across human, animal, and ecosystem sectors.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved pilot workshops in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia, conducted between March 2018 and December 2019. These workshops included 64 participants from central government ministries and subnational staff across human and animal health, forestry, security, and disaster sectors.
analysis.methods: The JRA process was developed through iterative co-development with country pilots and international experts. Existing sector-specific risk assessment methods were reviewed for suitability, and standardized feedback forms were used to collect anonymous input from participants.
analysis.main_results: The pilot workshops demonstrated the utility of the JRA process and provided critical feedback for its improvement. Key findings included the value of policy-level risk framing, the importance of political will, the need for subnational engagement, and the necessity of clear, stepwise guidance for efficient collaboration.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of the JRA process's effectiveness in facilitating multisectoral collaboration and improving risk assessment tools. The novelty lies in the co-development approach that integrates stakeholder feedback and expert input into a standardized, operational framework.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of operational tools for multisectoral risk assessment, supporting more effective and equitable collaboration across public health, animal health, and environmental sectors in managing zoonotic diseases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on feedback from pilot workshops, which may not fully represent broader contexts. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on qualitative feedback and iterative improvements rather than quantitative data.

analysis.summary_en: This study describes the development and testing of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) operational tool through pilot workshops in Indonesia, Tanzania, and Georgia. The JRA process was designed to be a standard, systematic, and qualitative method for assessing joint priority zoonotic disease hazards, incorporating expert opinion and sector-specific risk assessments. The pilot workshops highlighted the importance of policy-level risk framing, political will, subnational engagement, and clear guidance for effective collaboration. The findings suggest that the JRA tool can support multisectoral risk assessment and training, but the evidence is based on qualitative feedback and iterative improvements, limiting its strength. The study contributes to the field by demonstrating the feasibility of co-developing operational tools for zoonotic disease risk management.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在开发一种联合风险评估(JRA)的操作工具来管理人畜共患疾病,因为有效的多部门风险评估对于解决人类、动物和生态系统部门的健康风险至关重要。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究于 2018 年 3 月至 2019 年 12 月期间在印度尼西亚、坦桑尼亚联合共和国和格鲁吉亚举办了试点研讨会。这些研讨会有 64 名来自中央政府部委以及人类和动物健康、林业、安全和灾害部门的地方工作人员参加。
elements_zh.methods: JRA 流程是通过与国家试点和国际专家反复共同开发而制定的。对现有特定部门风险评估方法的适用性进行了审查,并使用标准化反馈表收集参与者的匿名意见。
elements_zh.main_results: 试点研讨会展示了 JRA 流程的实用性,并为其改进提供了重要的反馈。主要调查结果包括政策层面风险框架的价值、政治意愿的重要性、地方参与的必要性以及有效合作的明确、逐步指导的必要性。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为 JRA 流程在促进多部门合作和改进风险评估工具方面的有效性的证据。新颖之处在于共同开发方法,它将利益相关者的反馈和专家的意见整合到标准化的操作框架中。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为多部门风险评估操作工具的开发提供了信息,支持公共卫生、动物健康和环境部门在管理人畜共患疾病方面进行更有效和公平的合作。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于它依赖于试点研讨会的反馈,而这些反馈可能无法完全代表更广泛的背景。证据是中等的,因为它基于定性反馈和迭代改进而不是定量数据。
